newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Home starts, Philly survey due.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK --Home starts, Philly survey due.

text.p: Bond market players looked to the housing sector for clues of U.S. economic strength on Thursday with little other data expected.

The Department of Commerce was expected to report January housing starts rebounded to an annual rate of 1.42 million at 0830 EST/1330 GMT. Harsh weather helped pull the December figure down to 1.329 million.
The only other data are initial weekly jobless claims at the same time as housing starts and the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia's February business index.

It was questionable how much upside was left in the market after bonds failed to rally Wednesday on the back of yet another number suggesting inflation was contained. The Labor Department reported that consumer prices rose only 0.1 percent in January.

"The good news on inflation has passed and the market's taking a breather. People are taking profits and setting positions ahead of next week's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony," said Don Fine, chief market analyst at Chase Asset Management.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan testifies before Congress on February 26 and 27.
Fine said housing starts should outperform December's reading, but still not be as strong as they were in November. Initial claims also will be closely watched.

"Claims have been suggesting there's strength in the labor market. This is a volatile figure, but the four-week moving average has been coming down and probably will continue for at least another week," Fine said.

At 1000 EST/1500 GMT the Philadelphia Fed will release its February business survey which economists polled by Reuters expected, on average, to fall to 10.0 from 11.3 last month. Little market impact was seen on the number.

Tim O'Neill, chief economist at Bank of Montreal, said the CPI number virtually eliminated any chance of a Fed tightening at the March 25 policy makers meeting. The Fed will not tighten until it sees solid evidence of rising inflation tensions, O'Neill said, and to date it has seen none outside a modest uptrend in wages that most businesses can easily absorb amid booming profits.
O'Neill also noted the lack of forward momentum in the Treasury market following the weak inflation number and said players appeared to be content to consolidate last week's sizable gains.

"It appears the bond market has sort of hit a brick wall. The Fed is still seen as having a tightening bias and most economists think the warning lights on inflation will start flashing soon," said Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities International Inc.

Brusca said market participants may be coming to the conclusion that the news on inflation has been good, but it most likely will not stay that way. The best-case scenario is for inflation not to fall further, but to stay at current levels, Brusca said.
"There's nothing going on we would classically link to inflation, but remember the January numbers are the least reliable due to the weather. It has almost a hallucinatory effect," he said.
Food prices, for example, were expected to go back up after a weak January reading and air fares were notoriously volatile. Both contributed to weak January CPI, Brusca said.
